newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Observers deem Bosnia vote success, await results.
newsitem.headline: Observers deem Bosnia vote success, await results.

text.p: The first results from Bosnia's post-war election, praised by international organisers as widely free of violence and fraud, are expected on Monday.

Supervisors of the first national vote in a country ravaged by 43 months of war said independent monitors found the elections largely free and fair, all but dismissing a Moslem refusal to accept results from Serb areas.
Preliminary results from balloting for a three-person Bosnian presidency from Moslem, Serb and Croat communities as well as inter-ethnic parliaments are due on Monday.
They are expected to confirm the dominance of the three nationalist parties that led Bosnia into war.
U.S. President Bill Clinton praised the relatively peaceful election, but said the job of building democracy was not finished and the United States would do its part to help.

"Our commitment to Bosnia does not end with these elections," Clinton said. "We will continue to do our part to hold Bosnia's leaders to their commitments and to turn the promise of more than nine months ago in Dayton into a reality," he said, referring to the Bosnia peace agreement reached in Dayton, Ohio, last November.
He did not specifically address the role of U.S. troops or the politically-sensitive issue of their scheduled withdrawal by December 20, a year after their current mission started.
France and Germany joined Richard Holbrooke, U.S. architect of Bosnia's peace process who witnessed Saturday's polling, in praising the elections.

International sponsors have braced for post-election protests and obstruction by Bosnian factions which are still polarised, but said they are confident any disputes will be ironed out in coming days.
Earlier the Moslems refused to accept results from Serb areas because of alleged Serb ballot fraud.
Bosnian Serbs responded to the Moslems' move by ordering local election committees to stop counting votes in Serb areas, for which tens of thousands of Moslem refugees cast ballots.
But the counting resumed a few hours later following intervention by the election overseers, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

OSCE said all of Bosnia's factions knew in advance the elections would not be perfect and the preliminary evidence gave no cause to annul the results in any of the divided Moslem, Croat and Serb-dominated sectors.
"They were almost entirely free of abuse," said OSCE spokeswoman Agota Kuperman.
A monitors' report will influence a decision later this month on whether to certify the results. Steps to form power-sharing institutions and pass a 1997 budget would then begin.

Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic will meet Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in Paris for talks on building peace and normalising relations between Bosnia and rump Yugoslavia. The French Foreign Ministry said they may meet at the end of this week.
